explanation: If first is x+y and second is y+x, doubling first gives x+y+x+y, which contains y+x across the joining point. One search in the doubled string checks every split without testing each split separately.
correctness: Any rotation y+x appears in (x+y)+(x+y). Conversely, a length-n substring of first+first beginning in the first n positions consists of a suffix of first followed by its complementary prefix, so it is a rotation. Equality of positive lengths rules out shorter substrings and enforces the specified empty-input policy.
walkthrough: For 'orbit' and 'bitor', doubling gives 'orbitorbit'. Its length-five substring beginning at index 2 is 'bitor', so the answer is true. 'obrit' has the same characters but never occurs in the doubled text and is not a rotation.
timeComplexity: O(n + S(2n,n)) time, where S(h,p) is the runtime's substring-search cost. A conservative worst-case bound for an unspecified search implementation is O(n^2); do not assume a linear search guarantee in every language.
spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary space for the doubled string, plus any internal substring-search workspace.
edgeCases: Two empty strings return false; unequal lengths return false.
A rearrangement need not be a cyclic rotation.
